# Control API rejections

Error classes describe work that failed inside the graph. This page describes
the other half: the synchronous rejections the control API returns to a caller
before any work starts. A client library has to handle these, and they do not
all look alike.

## There is no single error envelope

Four different response shapes come back off `/v1`. Write your decoder for
all four.

**1. The flat string envelope.** The core families — templates, tags,
instances, nodes, runs, messages, assets, auth, admin — answer:

```json
{"error": "template has active instances"}
```

There is no `code`, no `error_code`, no `type`. The only thing that varies
machine-readably is the HTTP status. Switch on the status, not on the body.

**2. The nested object envelope.** The whole `/v1/observability/…` family
answers:

```json
{"error": {"code": "not_found", "message": "…"}}
```

`error` is a **string** on one half of the versioned surface and an **object**
on the other. The codes this family uses are `bad_request`, `not_found` and
`internal`. An optional `details` object may accompany them. This is the only
machine-readable code anywhere on the API.

**3. The JSON-RPC envelope.** `POST /v1/mcp` answers in JSON-RPC form, not in
either shape above.

**4. No JSON at all.** An unmatched path under `/v1` answers `404 page not
found` as `text/plain`. A wrong method on a matched path answers `405` with an
empty body. A decoder that assumes JSON on every non-2xx will throw on both.

**One route is not one shape.** `GET /v1/observability/instances/{id}`
answers the flat string envelope on 401 — the auth middleware runs before the
handler — and the nested object envelope on 404. Do not key your decoder on
the route.

## Fields that appear and disappear by status

Inside the flat envelope, extra fields come and go:

| Status | Extra fields |
| --- | --- |
| 401 | `denial_reason` |
| 403 | none — the body is `{"error": "permission denied"}` |
| 409 on `POST /v1/templates/{id}/undeploy` and asset delete | `active_count` |
| 400 on template register and validate | `validation_errors`, `validation_warnings`, and `warnings_as_errors` when that query flag was used |
| 422 or 502 from a claim-producer call | `producer_name`, `error_class`, `message` |

Treat every one of these as optional.

## Status codes

The conventional four mappings mostly hold: no token or an invalid token gives
401, an insufficiently privileged key gives 403 on a write route, a
well-formed unknown id gives 404, and a conflicting write gives 409. Three
places depart, and each will bite a client library.

**An unknown id does not always give 404.** `GET
/v1/instances/{unknown-uuid}/messages` answers **200 with an empty list**, and
so does `GET /v1/claim-handles/{unknown-uuid}/holders`. These routes filter by
id rather than resolving it, so a caller cannot distinguish "this instance has
no messages" from "there is no such instance". If you need that distinction,
resolve the instance first with `GET /v1/instances/{idOrKey}`.

**A malformed `?cursor=` gives 500, not 400.** It is client input, and it
answers `500` with the internal message in the body — on `/v1/instances`,
`/v1/templates`, `/v1/events`, `/v1/audit` and `/v1/observability/instances`.
Retry-on-5xx logic loops forever on a request that can never succeed. Either
only ever send a `next_cursor` the API itself returned, or treat a 500 whose
body mentions the cursor as terminal.

**An instance key on an `{id}`-spelled route gives 400.** Routes spelled
`{idOrKey}` accept either a UUID or the instance key and answer 404 for an
unknown one. Routes spelled `{id}` accept only a UUID, and answer **400** for
a key. `GET /v1/instances/{idOrKey}` and `GET /v1/instances/{id}/messages` are
siblings with different addressing rules.

## `denial_reason` on a 401

The 401 body carries a `denial_reason` naming why the request was refused.
The values are:

| Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `no_token` | No `Authorization` header, and the deployment is not in anonymous mode. |
| `invalid_token` | The bearer token matched no key. |
| `expired_token` | The key exists and its expiry has passed. |
| `revoked_token` | The key exists and was revoked. |
| `permission_denied` | Recorded on the audit trail for a 403; the 403 body itself carries no reason. |
| `invalid_dry_run` | The dry-run request flag was malformed. |
| `body_unreadable` | The request body could not be read. |
| `body_too_large` | The request body exceeded the accepted size. |

`expired_token` and `revoked_token` are worth distinguishing in a client: one
is fixed by rotating, the other by minting.

## Template registration rejections

`POST /v1/templates` and `POST /v1/templates/validate` reject with 400 and a
body that is worth reading in full:

```json
{
  "error": "template validation failed",
  "validation_errors": [{"path": "nodes[0].error_types[x].action", "msg": "…"}],
  "validation_warnings": [{"path": "…", "msg": "…"}]
}
```

`validation_errors` blocks the register. `validation_warnings` does **not** —
a register that returns 200 or 201 can still carry warnings, and the
error-class vocabulary warnings described elsewhere in this set arrive that
way. Read `validation_warnings` on success, not only on failure.

Pass `?warnings_as_errors=true` to make warnings block the register. The 400
body then carries `warnings_as_errors: true` so you can tell which rule
rejected you.

Two related notes:

- A registry lookup failure during validation answers **500**, with a body
  saying so explicitly: `template validation could not consult the service
  registry (transient infrastructure fault, not a validation failure)`. That
  one *is* worth retrying.
- `rimsky template lint` and `POST /v1/templates/validate` catch everything
  registration rejects, but neither is an offline check. The lint verb uploads
  the template and the control API does the work, so it needs a reachable
  deployment and its findings depend on which deployment you ask — the same
  file can lint clean against one and fail against another, because the
  answer depends on that deployment's executors and claim producers.

## Claim-producer errors passed through

When a request reaches a claim producer and the producer fails, the API passes
the producer's own error through rather than flattening it:

```json
{
  "error": "…",
  "producer_name": "claim-producer-postgres",
  "error_class": "pg/claim_unavailable",
  "message": "…"
}
```

The status is **422** when the producer's failure was a caller-side one
(invalid argument, failed precondition, out of range, not found, already
exists, permission denied) and **502** otherwise. The `error_class` field
here holds the same producer-declared class you would key `error_types` on —
see [acquire.md](acquire.md).

## Conflicts worth naming

| Situation | Status | Body |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Instance key already in use | 409 | flat envelope |
| Template still deployed when you try to delete it | 409 | `{"error": "template is in 'deployed' state; undeploy first"}` |
| Template has running instances when you undeploy or delete | 409 | flat envelope plus `active_count` |
| Instance already paused, or not paused when you resume | 409 | flat envelope |
| Moving a tag that is not allowed to move | 403 | flat envelope |
| Asset delete with in-flight holder runs | 409 | `{"error": "asset has in-flight holder runs; refuse delete", "active_count": n}` |
| Creating the deployment's first API key with an expiry | 400 | names `?force_expiring_key=true` as the confirmation |
| Revoking the last active key | 400 | names `?force_leave_anonymous=true` as the confirmation |

The last two are guard rails rather than faults: the API is refusing to let
you silently return the deployment to anonymous mode, and the body names the
query parameter that confirms you meant it.
